name: Sam Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Sam Larsen, 43, a senior loader operator at a large mine. I inspect the machine, move ore, then brief the next crew; I prefer a steady routine and do not use AI tools.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you value about the work, and what weighs on you at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing what a good loader sounds like and helping a new operator get the checks right. My partner Elise works at a bus depot; we have two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to keep doing the walk-around, even if a report takes less time. The machine does not get safer because a screen says the boxes are complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card leaves our pay alone, and most of my shift is in the cab. My partner Elise works at the bus depot, and we have about four months of expenses saved, so the mortgage does not depend only on overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the loader routine as it is and ask the planner to run the new report beside the paper board. I would not buy anything or change shifts until I had seen it used for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly comfortable about the job in this picture. I still wonder whether management will turn a small saving into pressure to do more with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household cost would you check first if a shift were lost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the mortgage and the children's school costs, then pause our plan to replace the fence. I would wait for two pay statements before moving money out of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the new report tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see the report match a real fault log across several shifts. If it misses one warning, I would ask the supervisor to keep a worker's signature on the check.

say: I would keep the **walk-around** even if a report takes less time.
I would not treat a complete screen as proof of a safe **machine**.
think: Most of my shift is in the **cab**, and pay is unchanged.
I count on Elise’s depot wage and our **four-month reserve**.
do: Keep the loader routine and compare the report beside the **paper board**.
Wait a month before changing **shifts** or buying anything.
feel: I feel **comfortable** about my job, though I watch for pressure to reduce crew size.
S0.quote: The machine does not get safer because a screen says the boxes are complete.
fieldNote: Sam trusts the established **walk-around** more than a new report.
His household has an outside wage and a **four-month reserve**.
He waits to see how management uses time saved before changing his **routine**.

steps.text: Keep the loader walk-around and current checks
Compare the report against the paper board for one month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the software will do more shift plans and checking, but the loader still needs an operator. We should not be asked to match a target until a person has checked how it was made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I assign some shifts and read service notes, so a piece of my senior work can move to software. The physical part is still most of my hours, but a few lost lead shifts would hit the mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd attend the mine's basic report training after the supervisor says which system is staying. I would ask to keep a weekly equipment check in my duties rather than take a private course on a tool that may change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the planning side and the speed of the new targets. I am not ready to leave work, but I would not call my hours certain either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which newer operator would you check on first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check on the newest operator first because a new target can leave them with the worst shifts. I would ask the supervisor to explain changes to the whole crew, not one person at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before taking a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need to see a month of reports next to the machine logs before trusting them. I would ask the maintenance foreman to explain any difference in plain words.

say: I would say software will handle more **plans and checks**, but the loader needs an operator.
I would not accept a target until a person checks how it was **made**.
think: I assign shifts and read service notes, so some **lead work** could move to software.
I can wait for a **proven system**.
I can wait for a proven system, but fewer shifts still affect the **family budget**.
do: Attend the mine’s basic **report training** after it chooses a system.
Ask to keep a weekly **equipment check** in my duties.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about targets and cannot call my hours certain.
S1.quote: I am not ready to leave work, but I would not call my hours certain either.
fieldNote: The hands-on job is steadier than Sam’s **planning duties**.
He wants the mine to choose a **system** before he spends effort learning it.
His concern is the possible loss of **lead shifts**, not immediate dismissal.

steps.text: Attend report training for the mine’s chosen system
Keep a weekly equipment inspection in my duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people the shift screens could be different by 2028, while robots for loader work come around 2031. The mine should give operators time to prepare for the physical change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead duties include shift allocation, which AGI can take quickly. The loader work lasts about three more years, but there are only some similar jobs nearby and I do not use AI tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union steward for transfer rules this month and find out which maintenance course the mine pays for. In 2029, I would take that course if it led to an open post and keep my loader shifts while I studied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels fast for someone who prefers the way things are done now. I am anxious about hours, though Elise's income and our savings give me some room to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your partner before paying for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Elise to compare the class schedule with the mortgage and the children's activities. I would not use our reserve for a course unless the mine confirmed it was paid and recognized.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, the first year after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there were no place in the course during 2029, I would keep my shifts and ask the maintenance lead whether I could shadow one inspection. I would wait for an internal vacancy rather than quit first.

say: I expect shift screens could change by **2028**, while loader robots come around 2031.
I want operators to have time to prepare for the **physical change** too.
think: I know AGI could take my **shift allocation** quickly.
I see only some similar jobs **nearby**, and I do not use AI tools now.
do: Ask the union steward for **transfer rules** this month.
Take a mine-paid maintenance course in 2029 if it leads to an **open post**.
feel: Two years feels **fast**, though Elise’s income and savings give me room to act.
S2.quote: The loader work lasts about three more years, but there are only some similar jobs nearby and I do not use AI tools now.
fieldNote: Sam is wary of AI and would use **union guidance** for transfer options.
The roughly three-year robot delay buys time but not a permanent **safe role**.
He will not spend his reserve unless the training leads to an **open job**.

steps.text: Ask the union steward about mine transfer rules
Take the paid maintenance course if a post is linked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to move toward maintenance before AGI arrives in 2031. Robots come around 2034, so I would want the mine to show which repair work still needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning part of my job could be gone by 2031, while I might keep operating equipment for another three years. I would learn a proven maintenance task, though I do not assume inspection will stay human forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the mine's maintenance certificate over the next few years and ask to shadow the crew that services pumps. In 2032, I would apply for a posted repair role if the vacancy and pay were clear, while keeping my loader shifts until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years is enough to ask better questions than the fast case allows. I would feel worse if the mine called a course preparation but had no job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of maintenance work might remain human?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which repairs require a person to work near the equipment and which may be handled by robots later. I want to learn a real task, not just move paperwork to a different desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2032, the first year after AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I would apply for a repair post only if it was funded and involved equipment work. If not, I would keep operating and check openings at another mine nearby.

say: I think five years gives us time to move toward **maintenance** before 2031.
I would ask which repairs still need a **person**.
think: My planning duties could go by 2031, while loader work may last until **2034**.
I would learn a proven task, but inspection is not **permanent protection**.
do: Take the mine maintenance **certificate** and shadow pump service workers.
Apply in 2032 for a funded repair role with clear **pay**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years lets me ask for a real job path.
S3.quote: I want to learn a real task, not just move paperwork to a different desk.
fieldNote: He prefers **hands-on maintenance** to a desk transfer.
Sam asks whether the work itself can later be done by **robots**.
He requires a funded vacancy and clear **pay** before changing roles.

steps.text: Complete the mine maintenance certificate and shadow pump repairs
Apply for a funded equipment repair post in 2032
Keep loader shifts until the repair offer is firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that ten years lets us prepare if the mine shares dates and training places. AGI comes in 2036 and robots reach loader work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 at AGI and 56 when robots follow, and I will still need a wage. I can try maintenance, but I do not know whether those jobs will last after the machines improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my loader job while completing the maintenance certificate and save part of my overtime each month. In 2037, I would apply for a repair post only if the mine confirmed it still needed a person on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning makes me feel more settled than two years does. I still do not want to rely on savings for a long gap between jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How might your children’s plans change by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2037, our children will be young adults, and Elise and I would ask what training they want before paying for anything. I would not assume they should follow me into mining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2037, the first year after AGI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check whether other mines still have open equipment roles and compare the pay before a move. I would not move the family for a job that was only a forecast.

say: I see ten years to prepare if the mine shares **dates** and training places.
I know loader robots may arrive around **2039**.
think: At 53 and 56, I will still need a **wage**.
I would try maintenance, but I do not know whether those jobs are **lasting**.
do: Complete the maintenance certificate while keeping my **loader job**.
Save overtime and apply for a confirmed repair **post** in 2037.
feel: The long warning feels **settling**, but I do not want a long gap without wages.
S4.quote: I would not move the family for a job that was only a forecast.
fieldNote: Sam uses the decade for training while maintaining **current income**.
He expects the children to be young adults and seeks their input on **training**.
He would move only for a real **post**, not a forecast.

steps.text: Finish the mine maintenance certificate while operating
Apply for a confirmed repair job in 2037
Ask the young adult children what training they want

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because shift planning may change before I can finish a course. Paid training, a fair transfer process and a real vacancy would help me choose a next step.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want managers to show workers the timetable and the jobs attached to each course. I can learn a new system when I know what it is for, but I do not want to be rushed into a guess.

headlineQuote: Paid training, a fair transfer process and a real vacancy would help me choose a next step.
portrait: Sam is a 43-year-old senior mine operator with a **technical diploma**.
He trusts familiar routines and takes time to adopt **new systems**.
His partner works at a bus depot; they have a mortgage and **four months saved**.
He will consider maintenance training when it leads to a **funded vacancy**, not a promise.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries him because it changes shift planning before a course can be completed.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training**, fair transfer terms and a real vacancy would help Sam choose a next step.
